title: Understanding Your Construction Worker Salary: Hourly to Annual Conversion
description: Learn how to convert your construction worker salary from hourly to annual, including 38-hour weeks, fortnightly pay, tax, and super. Use our timesheet tool to estimate your pay.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time worker on 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual salary before tax and super. Remember that this assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave entitlements. If you are a casual construction worker, your total hourly rate is your base rate plus 25%. For example, if the base rate is $30.00, casual loading adds $7.50, making your total $37.50 per hour. Super is calculated on the total ordinary earnings, including casual loading.

faqs.q: How much super will I receive as a construction worker?
faqs.a: Your employer must pay super guarantee of 12% on your ordinary earnings, paid on top of your salary. For a construction worker earning the industry average of $1985.30 per week, super would be approximately $238.24 per week, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Salary

If you're a construction worker trying to understand your **construction worker salary**, the first step is converting your hourly rate to an annual figure. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For most full-time employees, the typical working week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Act. So the calculation becomes:

**Annual salary ≈ hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks**

For example, if your hourly rate is $35.00, your annual salary would be approximately $35 × 38 × 52 = $69,160 before tax and super. This estimate assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It's a starting point for budgeting and comparing job offers.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many construction workers are paid fortnightly. To find your gross fortnightly pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by two. Using the example above, weekly pay is $35 × 38 = $1,330, so fortnightly pay is $2,660. This can help you manage your cash flow and compare with pay slips.

## Industry Average for Construction Workers

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Average Weekly Earnings for May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings in the construction industry are $1,985.30 per week. This is an industry average, not a median for your specific job. Your actual **construction worker salary** may be higher or lower depending on your role, experience, location, and award coverage. Use this figure as a benchmark, but always check your own pay rate.

Using the industry average, the annual salary would be $1,985.30 × 52 = approximately $103,235.60. This is before tax and super. Remember that this average includes all full-time construction workers, from labourers to managers.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage, which from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual workers receive an additional 25% loading, making their minimum $33.05 per hour. However, most construction workers are covered by modern awards or enterprise agreements that set higher minimum rates. For example, the Building and Construction General On-site Award 2020 specifies pay rates for different classifications. Always check your award or agreement to ensure you're being paid correctly.

### Casual Loading

If you work as a casual construction worker, your employer must pay casual loading of 25% on top of your base hourly rate. This compensates for not receiving paid leave such as annual leave or sick leave. When using our [timesheet](/), you can enter your base hourly rate and check a box to add 25% casual loading. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool will calculate it for you.

## Tax on Your Construction Worker Salary

Your annual salary is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Additionally, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. For a construction worker earning the industry average of $103,235.60, the tax would be approximately $24,267 (using the 30% bracket) plus Medicare of $2,065, leaving a take-home pay of around $76,904. However, this is a rough estimate. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a more detailed calculation.

## Superannuation Guarantee

Your employer must pay super guarantee of 12% on your ordinary earnings, paid on top of your salary. For a construction worker earning $1,985.30 per week, super would be $238.24 per week, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution that goes into your super fund. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

## Using Our Tools

To estimate your own **construction worker salary**, start with our [the timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate, select your hours per week (default 38), and optionally add casual loading. The tool will show your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross pay, plus estimated tax and super. You can also explore [pay guides](/blog) for award rates or [reference tables](/data) for industry averages.

Remember that the figures provided are estimates. For a precise determination of your pay, consult your employer, your award, or the Fair Work Ombudsman. The Australian Taxation Office provides official tax calculators. Always verify your own circumstances.

### Key Takeaways

- Annual salary = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 (assume 38 hours for full-time)
- Fortnightly pay = weekly pay × 2
- Construction industry average weekly earnings: $1,985.30 (full-time ordinary time, May 2026) – this is an industry average, not a job median
- National Minimum Wage: $26.44/hour; casual rate $33.05/hour including 25% loading
- Super guarantee: 12% paid on top of ordinary earnings, up to $270,830 per year
- Tax: use 2026–27 resident rates with Medicare levy of 2%

For more detailed information, see our [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page or [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page. If you need to convert a salary to an hourly rate, visit our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) guide. Casual workers can check [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) rules. For job-specific pay data, see [job pay](/topics/job-pay).
